headline: Maintain the smallest tail for each subsequence length
statement: Return the length of a longest strictly increasing subsequence of nums. A subsequence preserves index order but may skip elements.
intuition: For each possible length, remember the smallest ending value of an increasing subsequence seen so far. A smaller ending is easier to extend with future values. Use binary search to replace the first saved ending that is at least the current number, or append a new ending.
approach: Keep tails sorted, where tails[k] is the smallest known ending of a length k+1 subsequence.
Binary-search the first tail >= the next value.
Replace that tail, or append if the value extends every known length.
correctness: If the first tail >= x is at index k, every earlier tail is smaller than x, so x can extend a length-k subsequence. Replacing the length k+1 tail with x improves or preserves extensibility without changing achievable lengths. If no such tail exists, x achieves one new length. Thus tails length equals the maximum achievable increasing length after every prefix.
bruteForce: List all 2^n subsequences. A simpler O(n²) DP instead checks every earlier smaller value for each endpoint.

complexity.explanation: Each of n values performs binary search among at most n tails.

pitfalls: Use lower bound (first >=), so equal numbers do not extend a strictly increasing sequence.
The contents of tails are summary minima, not necessarily a recovered subsequence.
